title: SWE-bench: Can Language Models Resolve Real GitHub Issues?
hook: Test a coding agent on real GitHub issues with real test suites - not toy problems - and the bar turns out to be much harder than HumanEval suggested.
key_points: 2,294 task instances drawn from 12 popular Python repos, each pairing a real issue description with the merged fix PR.
Success requires editing an unfamiliar, multi-file codebase so the project's existing tests pass - a realistic software engineering task.
Early evaluated models resolved only a small fraction of tasks, exposing a gap between code-generation benchmarks and real-world engineering.
Now a headline metric for coding agent systems and a driver of agent scaffolding research.
content_html: Jimenez and colleagues published SWE-bench in October 2023, arguing that function-level code generation benchmarks like HumanEval underestimate the difficulty of real software engineering. By collecting thousands of GitHub issues and their corresponding merged pull requests from popular open-source Python projects, they built a benchmark where a model must navigate an entire repository, understand existing code, and produce a patch that passes the project's test suite.
extra_html:
How it works

Each task instance provides the repository at the state before the fix, the natural-language issue description, and a set of pass/fail tests that the correct fix should satisfy. A model or agent must generate a code patch - potentially spanning multiple files - that resolves the issue. Evaluation runs the project's tests in a controlled environment; a task is solved only if the relevant tests go from failing to passing without breaking others.

Why it matters

SWE-bench reframed the capability question from "can a model write a function" to "can a model act as a software engineer on a real project." The low initial solve rates spurred development of agent scaffolding, retrieval-augmented code editing, and tool-use frameworks. It is now a standard leaderboard for coding agent systems. Read the benchmark design and baseline results in the paper on arXiv.

related.title: Codex: Evaluating Large Language Models Trained on Code
related.hook: Fine-tune GPT on public GitHub code and you get a model that solves programming problems and powers GitHub Copilot - plus a new benchmark, HumanEval, that tests functional correctness.

related.title: MMLU: Measuring Massive Multitask Language Understanding
related.hook: Want one number for how broadly an LLM 'knows stuff'? MMLU is a 57-subject exam spanning history, law, medicine, and math — and it became a default yardstick.

related.title: HELM: Holistic Evaluation of Language Models
related.hook: A single accuracy number hides a lot. HELM evaluates language models across many scenarios and many metrics at once — and reports it all in the open.

related.title: ReAct: Reasoning + Acting
related.hook: Thinking alone can drift; acting alone is blind. ReAct interleaves reasoning with tool calls so an LLM can plan, look things up, and correct course — the template for agents.

flashcards.prompt: When is a SWE-bench task counted as solved?

choices.text: When the relevant tests go from failing to passing without breaking others
When the patch matches the merged PR token-for-token
When any single test in the repo passes
